set1.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set1.q: A 63-year-old with severe kyphoscoliosis has a respiratory acidosis. Which group of causes does his deformity belong to?
opts: Circulatory disorders
The circulatory causes are congestive heart failure and shock; kyphoscoliosis is a chest wall cause.
Chest wall dysfunction
Correct. Causes of respiratory acidosis include chest wall dysfunction (thoracic cage deformities, kyphoscoliosis), airway obstruction and circulatory disorders.
Airway obstruction
Airway obstruction covers extrathoracic tumors, asthma, bronchitis and emphysema; kyphoscoliosis is chest wall dysfunction.
Respiratory center depression
Respiratory depression is from drugs such as opioids, barbiturates and anesthetics; kyphoscoliosis is chest wall dysfunction.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 25, 26 and 27

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 64-year-old's blood gas reports a base deficit. Bicarbonate is half of his whole blood buffer base. Which anions make up the other half?
opts: Sodium and potassium
Sodium and potassium are cations, not anions; the buffer base is anions: bicarbonate plus plasma proteins and phosphates.
Proteins and phosphates
Correct. Base excess (whole blood buffer base) is the sum of the buffer anions in whole blood: bicarbonate is half, and other anions such as plasma proteins and phosphates are the other half.
Chloride and sulfate
Chloride is the measured anion of the anion gap and sulfate an unmeasured one; the other half of the buffer base is plasma proteins and phosphates.
Lactate and ketoacids
Lactate and ketoacids are acids whose excess produces a base deficit (and raise the anion gap); the other half of the buffer base is plasma proteins and phosphates.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 40, 41 and 45

set1.io: Explain differences between arterial and venous blood gas measurements.
set1.q: A 62-year-old's venous sample was drawn from an arm with an infection at the puncture site. Why might it mislead about her overall gases?
opts: Local infection affects only arterial samples
It is venous blood that can be affected by local infection, temperature, perfusion and movement; arterial blood is the better mixture.
Venous blood is a better mixture than arterial
The reverse: arterial blood provides the better mixture, while venous blood is localized to the phlebotomy site.
Venous blood reflects local conditions at its site
Correct. Venous blood gives information localized to the phlebotomy site and can be affected by temperature, perfusion, movement and local infection; arterial blood is a better mixture.
Venous carbon dioxide is lower than arterial
Venous carbon dioxide pressure runs higher (41 to 57 mm Hg against 35 to 45); the concern here is local effects on the venous sample.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 5 and 11

set1.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set1.q: A 26-year-old is anxious and breathing fast: pH 7.52 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), carbon dioxide pressure 28 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate 24 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which disorder is this?
opts: Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis has a low pH and a decreased bicarbonate; his pH is high with a normal bicarbonate.
Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory acidosis has a pH below 7.35 and a HIGH carbon dioxide; his pH is high and carbon dioxide low.
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis has an increased bicarbonate with a normal carbon dioxide; his bicarbonate is normal and his carbon dioxide low.
Respiratory alkalosis
Correct. Respiratory alkalosis: pH above 7.45, carbon dioxide low, bicarbonate normal; anxiety stimulates the respiratory center and hyperventilation depletes the carbon dioxide.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 30, 29 and 33

set1.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set1.q: A 52-year-old has an arterial pH of 7.30 (normal 7.35 to 7.45) and a carbon dioxide pressure of 56 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg). What does the carbon dioxide tell you about the acidosis?
opts: It shows a mixed acidosis and alkalosis
A high carbon dioxide pressure with a low pH is the straight respiratory acidosis pattern; nothing here points the other way.
It is fully compensated
Compensation moves pH back toward normal; here the pH is low with a high carbon dioxide, the primary respiratory pattern.
Its primary problem is respiratory
Correct. A primary respiratory disorder is a problem with the carbon dioxide pressure and the lungs: a high carbon dioxide pressure with a low pH is respiratory acidosis.
Its primary problem is metabolic
A metabolic disorder's primary problem is the bicarbonate (and nonvolatile acids and the kidney); a raised carbon dioxide with a low pH points to the lungs.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 50, 51 and 27

set1.io: Calculate the anion gap.
set1.q: A 49-year-old's serum sodium is 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 148 mEq/L), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 24 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
opts: 12 mEq/L
Correct. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 140 minus (104 plus 24) = 140 minus 128 = 12, inside the normal 9 to 15.
36 mEq/L
36 is sodium minus chloride alone (140 minus 104); the bicarbonate must be added to the chloride before subtracting: 140 minus 128 = 12.
60 mEq/L
60 adds the bicarbonate back (140 minus 104 plus 24); the formula subtracts the SUM of chloride and bicarbonate: 140 minus 128 = 12.
116 mEq/L
116 subtracts only the bicarbonate (140 minus 24); both chloride and bicarbonate are subtracted: 140 minus 128 = 12.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set1.q: A 34-year-old is found unresponsive after taking narcotics. His carbon dioxide pressure is 62 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg). Which mechanism explains the value?
opts: Hyperventilation from pain or anxiety
Pain and anxiety cause hyperventilation and a LOW carbon dioxide pressure; his is high, from respiratory center depression.
Pulmonary emboli
Pulmonary emboli are a cause of a low carbon dioxide pressure; the high value after narcotics is from an impaired respiratory center.
Airway obstruction from obstructive lung disease
Emphysema, asthma and chronic bronchitis raise the carbon dioxide too, but nothing suggests lung disease; the narcotics impair the respiratory center.
Impaired function of the respiratory center
Correct. Causes of an elevated carbon dioxide pressure include impaired function of the respiratory center: anesthesia, drugs such as narcotics and barbiturates, and head trauma.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

mis.Airway obstruction from obstructive lung: competing cause, not in this case

set1.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set1.q: A 45-year-old's blood pH stays within very narrow limits. Which organs primarily keep the acid-base balance there?
opts: The liver and the kidneys
The liver is not named among the buffering systems; they are primarily the lungs and the kidneys.
The lungs and the liver
The lungs are one primary system, but the other is the kidneys, not the liver.
The bones and the blood
Bones and blood buffer only to a smaller extent; the primary buffering systems are the lungs and the kidneys.
The lungs and the kidneys
Correct. The body's acid-base balance is kept within very narrow parameters by buffering systems, primarily the lungs and kidneys, and to a smaller extent the bones and blood.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 72-year-old woman in the intensive care unit has an arterial blood gas drawn. Which venous blood studies is it often used in combination with?
opts: A lipid panel and cardiac troponin
These are not the studies the blood gas is combined with; the venous analysis paired with it is the complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel.
A blood count and a metabolic panel

Correct. The blood gas is often used with other assessments: vital signs, the physical examination, venous blood analysis such as the complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, fluid intake and urine output.
Blood cultures and a sputum culture
Cultures are not among the assessments paired with the blood gas; it is used with vital signs, the examination, the complete blood count and metabolic panel, intake and urine output.
A coagulation panel and a D-dimer
Clotting studies are not the companions of the blood gas; venous blood analysis such as the complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel is.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

set1.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set1.q: A 24-year-old is brought in after an opioid overdose: pH 7.25 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), carbon dioxide pressure 62 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate 24 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which disorder is this?
opts: Acute respiratory acidosis
Correct. Acute respiratory acidosis: pH below 7.35, carbon dioxide high, bicarbonate normal; respiratory depression from drugs such as opioids, barbiturates and anesthetics is the cause.
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis has a decreased bicarbonate and a normal carbon dioxide; his carbon dioxide is high with a normal bicarbonate.
Chronic respiratory acidosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis comes from long-standing lung or chest wall disease and shows a RISEN bicarbonate; his is normal.
Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis has a pH above 7.45 and a LOW carbon dioxide; his pH is low and his carbon dioxide high.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 27, 28 and 31

set1.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set1.q: A 47-year-old has had several days of vomiting. Which set of blood gas findings is expected before any compensation?
opts: High pH, low carbon dioxide, normal bicarbonate
That is respiratory alkalosis, from hyperventilation; vomiting loses acid and raises the bicarbonate.
Low pH, high carbon dioxide, high bicarbonate
That is chronic respiratory acidosis with compensation; vomiting produces a metabolic alkalosis.
Low pH, normal carbon dioxide, low bicarbonate
That is metabolic acidosis, as diarrhea causes through base loss; vomiting loses ACID and raises the pH.
High pH, normal carbon dioxide, high bicarbonate
Correct. Metabolic alkalosis: pH above 7.45, carbon dioxide normal, bicarbonate increased; vomiting causes it through acid loss.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 33, 34, 30 and 31

set1.io: Discuss the clinical significance of an abnormal anion gap.
set1.q: A 47-year-old with severe hyperlipidemia has an unexpectedly low anion gap. What explains it?
opts: Lipid skews the sodium and chloride
Correct. A decreased anion gap can be associated with severe hyperlipidemia, which affects the estimates of the sodium and chloride levels.
A decrease in unmeasured cations
Fewer unmeasured cations raise the gap; the low value here is from the lipid's effect on the sodium and chloride estimates.
A build-up of ketoacids in the blood
Ketoacids are unmeasured anions that raise the gap; hyperlipidemia lowers it through the sodium and chloride estimates.
An excess of unmeasured anions
Extra unmeasured anions RAISE the gap; severe hyperlipidemia lowers it by affecting the sodium and chloride estimates.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 48 and 47

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 41-year-old's arterial blood gas reports a partial pressure of oxygen. What does this value measure?
opts: Oxygen bound to hemoglobin
Bound oxygen is the 98% carried on hemoglobin, described by the saturation; the partial pressure measures the dissolved oxygen in plasma.
All the oxygen in the blood
The actual total amount of oxygen in the blood is the oxygen content; the partial pressure measures only the oxygen dissolved in plasma.
Hemoglobin's maximum oxygen load
The maximum amount of oxygen that can combine with hemoglobin is the oxygen capacity; the partial pressure measures dissolved oxygen.
Oxygen dissolved in the plasma
Correct. The partial pressure of oxygen is the pressure exerted by oxygen dissolved in blood plasma (less than 2% of the oxygen carried); 98% is bound to hemoglobin.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 13, 35 and 37

set1.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set1.q: A 71-year-old with a progressive neuromuscular disease has an arterial oxygen pressure of 62 mm Hg (normal greater than 80 mm Hg). Which cause on his chart explains it?
opts: Mechanical over-ventilation
Over-ventilation is hyperventilation, which raises the oxygen pressure; his neuromuscular disease causes hypoventilation.
An increased fraction of inspired oxygen
An increased fraction of inspired oxygen RAISES the oxygen pressure; his low value comes from hypoventilation.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation is a cause of an elevated oxygen pressure; neuromuscular weakness causes hypoventilation and a low one.
Hypoventilation from the neuromuscular disease

Correct. Causes of a low oxygen pressure include hypoventilation secondary to neuromuscular disease, with cardiac dysfunction, intracardiac shunts, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, restrictive lung disease and insufficient inspired oxygen.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 24 and 29

set1.io: Discuss indications for arterial blood gas testing.
set1.q: A 36-year-old with vomiting and confusion has an arterial blood gas ordered to evaluate her acid-base status. Which values does that evaluation rest on?
opts: pH, sodium and potassium
Sodium and potassium are electrolytes; acid-base status is evaluated from the pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide.
Oxygen, hemoglobin and hematocrit
These describe oxygenation and oxygen carriage; acid-base status rests on the pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide.
pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide
Correct. The blood gas evaluates acid-base status through the pH, the bicarbonate and the carbon dioxide; oxygenation (oxygen) and ventilation (carbon dioxide) are its other two assessments.
Bicarbonate, chloride and albumin
Chloride and albumin enter the anion gap; acid-base status itself is evaluated from the pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 3 and 45

set1.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set1.q: A 50-year-old with metabolic alkalosis from vomiting has a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L). How does the alkalosis itself move potassium?
opts: Into the urine, with no shift between spaces
pH changes cause changes in serum potassium by shifting it between spaces; alkalosis shifts it into the cells.
Out of the cells, raising the serum level
That is the acidosis pattern, a shift into the extracellular space with hyperkalemia; alkalosis moves potassium into the cells.
Into the cells, lowering the serum level
Correct. In alkalosis potassium shifts into the intracellular space, causing hypokalemia.
It leaves the potassium level unchanged
pH changes do change serum potassium: alkalosis shifts it into the intracellular space and causes hypokalemia.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Explain differences between arterial and venous blood gas measurements.
set1.q: A 50-year-old's venous blood gas shows a carbon dioxide pressure of 50 mm Hg (venous normal 41 to 57 mm Hg; arterial normal 35 to 45 mm Hg). How should the value be read?
opts: Low, from hyperventilation
Fifty is not low for either sample; for venous blood it sits inside the normal 41 to 57 mm Hg.
High, from carbon dioxide retention
Fifty would be high for an ARTERIAL sample (35 to 45), but this is venous blood, whose normal is 41 to 57 mm Hg.
Unreadable, as venous gases have no normal
Venous gases have their own normal values: carbon dioxide 41 to 57 mm Hg, so 50 is normal for venous blood.
Normal for a venous sample
Correct. Venous carbon dioxide pressure normally runs higher than arterial, 41 to 57 mm Hg, so 50 is normal for this venous sample.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 11

set1.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set1.q: A 59-year-old's arterial blood gas has just arrived. Taking a step-wise approach, which value is looked at first?
opts: The pH
Correct. The step-wise approach to any acid-base problem starts with the pH: low is acidosis, high is alkalosis. Then: which values are outside the normal range, and do the labs fit the patient?
The bicarbonate
Bicarbonate, the metabolic marker, comes after the pH; the step-wise approach begins with the pH.
The carbon dioxide pressure
The carbon dioxide pressure is read next, to point to a respiratory cause; the first question is: what is the pH?
The anion gap
The anion gap is calculated from the electrolytes later in the workup; the first step is the pH.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 49 and 21

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: The curves shown are a 44-year-old's oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve at three pH values. Besides a fall in pH, which change shifts the curve to the right?
opts: A fall in temperature
It is INCREASED temperature that shifts the curve to the right, with increased hydrogen ions, carbon dioxide and BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate).
A fall in carbon dioxide
Increased carbon dioxide is what shifts the curve right; a fall works the other way.
A rise in temperature
Correct. The curve shifts to the right with increased hydrogen ions (a lower pH), increased carbon dioxide, increased temperature and increased BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate).
A rise in pH
A high pH (alkalosis) shifts the curve to the LEFT, as the 7.6 curve lies; oxygen then bonds more tightly to hemoglobin.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 39
set1.alt: Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curves labeled pH 7.6, 7.4 and 7.2

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 38-year-old is treated after a house fire and has a carboxyhemoglobin of 18% (normal less than 2%). Why does carbon monoxide take oxygen's place on hemoglobin?
opts: It dissolves in plasma, where 98% of the oxygen travels
Only about 2% of oxygen is dissolved in plasma and 98% is bound to hemoglobin; carbon monoxide takes those binding sites with a 240-fold affinity.
Hemoglobin's affinity for it is 240 times that for oxygen
Correct. Carboxyhemoglobin forms when hemoglobin is exposed to carbon monoxide, and hemoglobin's affinity for carbon monoxide is 240 times its affinity for oxygen.
It shifts the dissociation curve to the right in acidosis
A right shift comes with acidosis and makes hemoglobin release oxygen more easily; carbon monoxide displaces oxygen through a 240-fold affinity.
It raises the fraction of inspired oxygen in the lungs
The fraction of inspired oxygen is the oxygen in the air taken into the lungs; carbon monoxide wins because hemoglobin's affinity for it is 240 times oxygen's.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 42, 13 and 39

set1.io: Discuss the clinical significance of an abnormal anion gap.
set1.q: A 58-year-old with cirrhosis has a low anion gap and a serum albumin of 2.5 g/dL (normal 4.5 g/dL). What must be done before the gap is interpreted?
opts: Correct it upward for the low albumin
Correct. A decreased anion gap can be associated with hypoalbuminemia; the gap must be corrected if albumin is abnormal, adding 2.5 mmol/L for each 1 g/dL of albumin below 4.5 g/dL.
Add the potassium into the formula
The anion gap formula is sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate); what changes here is the albumin correction, upward.
Read it as calculated; albumin is irrelevant
Albumin accounts for most of the normal anion gap, so the gap must be corrected when albumin levels are abnormal.
Correct it downward for the low albumin
The correction ADDS to the gap: 2.5 mmol/L for each 1 g/dL of albumin below 4.5 g/dL.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 48, 45 and 46

set1.io: Discuss indications for arterial blood gas testing.
set1.q: A 74-year-old's arterial blood gas comes back abnormal, and a student asks how sick he is from the numbers alone. What is the best reply?
opts: The bicarbonate alone grades his severity
No single value grades severity: the blood gas does not indicate the degree of an abnormality; examine the patient.
The gas cannot show the degree; examine him
Correct. The blood gas does NOT indicate the degree of any abnormality; a physical assessment is needed (treat the patient and not the labs).
The further from normal, the sicker he is
The blood gas does not indicate the degree of any abnormality; severity comes from a physical assessment of the patient.
A normal pH would rule out serious illness
The labs must be checked against the clinical presentation, and the gas does not show degree; the patient has to be assessed.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 5 and 49

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 49-year-old with asthma is seen in clinic, and the clinician wants only her oxygen saturation, not her pH or gas pressures. Besides the arterial blood gas, which test measures it?
opts: Base excess
Base excess is the sum of buffer anions in whole blood; it says nothing about saturation, which pulse oximetry also measures.
Pulse oximetry
Correct. Oxygen saturation, the ratio of hemoglobin's actual oxygen content to its maximum capacity, is also measured by pulse oximetry.
Venous oxygen content
Oxygen content is the actual amount of oxygen in the blood, not the saturation ratio; saturation is also measured by pulse oximetry.
Carboxyhemoglobin level
Carboxyhemoglobin indicates the amount of carbon monoxide poisoning; saturation is also measured by pulse oximetry.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 35, 37 and 42

set1.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set1.q: A 50-year-old with renal failure has a metabolic acidosis. Which set of blood gas findings is expected before any compensation?
opts: Low pH, high carbon dioxide, normal bicarbonate
That is acute respiratory acidosis, with the carbon dioxide as the primary problem; in metabolic acidosis the bicarbonate falls.
High pH, low carbon dioxide, normal bicarbonate
That is respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation; a metabolic acidosis has a low pH and a low bicarbonate.
Low pH, normal carbon dioxide, low bicarbonate
Correct. Metabolic acidosis: pH below 7.35, carbon dioxide normal, bicarbonate decreased; renal failure is an acid-gain cause.
High pH, normal carbon dioxide, high bicarbonate
That is metabolic alkalosis, from base gain or acid loss; renal failure adds acid and lowers the bicarbonate.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 31, 27, 33 and 30

set1.io: Explain differences between arterial and venous blood gas measurements.
set1.q: A 66-year-old's arterial blood gas sample is labeled for the lab. Which detail about him must be recorded with it?
opts: The arm his last venous sample came from
That has no bearing on the arterial sample; record room air or the supplemental oxygen, which directly affects the oxygen pressure.
The time of his last meal
Mealtime is not what the sample needs; it needs room air or the supplemental oxygen, because inspired oxygen directly affects the oxygen pressure.
Room air, or any supplemental oxygen he is on
Correct. Indicate whether the patient was breathing room air or describe any supplemental oxygen, because the oxygen pressure is directly affected by the fraction of inspired oxygen.
His blood pressure at the draw
Blood pressure is not recorded with the sample; whether he breathed room air or supplemental oxygen is, since it drives the oxygen pressure.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 13 and 36

set1.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set1.q: A 23-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has a low bicarbonate. Which change compensates for it?
opts: Faster breathing, lowering the carbon dioxide
Correct. Metabolic disorders are compensated by adjusting the ventilatory rate and carbon dioxide pressure (over minutes to hours); metabolic acidosis is compensated by a decrease in carbon dioxide.
Slower breathing, raising the carbon dioxide
A rise in carbon dioxide is the compensation for metabolic ALKALOSIS; acidosis is compensated by lowering it.
The kidneys excreting more bicarbonate
Losing bicarbonate would deepen the acidosis, and kidney adjustment compensates respiratory disorders; breathing lowers the carbon dioxide.
The kidneys reabsorbing more bicarbonate
Kidney bicarbonate adjustment, over days, compensates RESPIRATORY disorders; a metabolic acidosis is compensated through breathing.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 52, 53 and 50

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 27-year-old has an arterial pH of 7.56 (normal 7.35 to 7.45) after a long bout of vomiting. How does this pH change hemoglobin's hold on oxygen?
opts: Right shift: oxygen is released more easily
This is the acidosis pattern (low pH); a pH of 7.56 is an alkalosis, which shifts the curve left and holds oxygen more tightly.
Right shift: oxygen bonds more tightly
The right shift belongs to a low pH and loosens the bond; alkalosis shifts the curve left, with tighter bonding.
Left shift: oxygen is released more easily
A left shift means oxygen bonds more tightly, not that it is released more easily; easier release is the right shift of acidosis.
Left shift: oxygen bonds more tightly
Correct. A high pH (alkalosis) shifts the curve to the left, and oxygen bonds more tightly to hemoglobin.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set1.q: A 60-year-old has developed a respiratory acidosis. Over what time course do his kidneys compensate?
opts: It does not; only breathing compensates
Breathing compensates metabolic disorders; a respiratory disorder is compensated by the kidney, over days.
Over minutes to hours
Minutes to hours is the time course of compensation for a METABOLIC disorder, by adjusting the ventilatory rate and carbon dioxide.
Over days
Correct. Respiratory disorders are compensated by the kidney adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption, which occurs over days.
Within seconds
Kidney compensation is slow: it occurs over days, by adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 50 and 52

set1.io: Calculate the anion gap.
set1.q: A 34-year-old with several days of diarrhea has serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 148 mEq/L), potassium 3.4 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
opts: 6.6 mEq/L
6.6 also subtracts the potassium; the formula is sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) only: 138 minus 128 = 10.
10 mEq/L
Correct. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 138 minus (112 plus 16) = 138 minus 128 = 10, inside the normal 9 to 15; the potassium is not in the formula.
13.4 mEq/L
13.4 adds the potassium to the sodium; the formula uses sodium alone: 138 minus (112 plus 16) = 10.
26 mEq/L
26 is sodium minus chloride alone (138 minus 112); the bicarbonate must also be subtracted: 138 minus 128 = 10.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 58-year-old man has a head injury. His carbon dioxide pressure rises from 46 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) to 58 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), yet his breathing rate has not risen. Why is this a concern?
opts: Rising carbon dioxide should drive ventilation up
Correct. Carbon dioxide is the major chemical factor regulating ventilation: as it rises, ventilation increases. Head trauma impairs the respiratory center, so that response can fail.
His kidneys should have corrected it in minutes
Kidney compensation for a respiratory problem, by adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption, occurs over days; the expected fast response is increased ventilation.
Rising carbon dioxide should slow the breathing
The direction is reversed: as carbon dioxide rises, ventilation increases. A rate that does not rise points to an impaired respiratory center, as after head trauma.
Only a falling oxygen pressure drives ventilation
Carbon dioxide in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid is the major chemical factor regulating ventilation; its rise should have increased his breathing.
set1.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 10, 22 and 50

set2.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set2.q: A 57-year-old has a respiratory acidosis from an extrathoracic tumor narrowing his airway. Which group of causes is this?
opts: Chest wall dysfunction
Chest wall dysfunction means thoracic cage deformities such as kyphoscoliosis; a tumor narrowing the airway is airway obstruction.
Stimulation of the respiratory center
Stimulating the brainstem respiratory center causes respiratory ALKALOSIS; this is an obstructive cause of acidosis.
Circulatory disorders
Circulatory causes are congestive heart failure and shock; a tumor compressing the airway is obstruction.
Airway obstruction
Correct. Airway obstruction causes respiratory acidosis: extrathoracic tumors, asthma, bronchitis and emphysema.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: Explain differences between arterial and venous blood gas measurements.
set2.q: In a healthy 40-year-old, an arterial and a venous sample are drawn at the same moment. How does the venous sample compare?
opts: Lower carbon dioxide pressure and higher pH
Both are reversed: venous carbon dioxide pressure is higher (41 to 57 mm Hg) and venous pH lower (7.31 to 7.41) than arterial.
Higher oxygen content and higher pH
Venous oxygen content is lower (11 to 16 mL/dL against arterial 15 to 22) and venous pH is lower too.
Higher carbon dioxide pressure and lower pH
Correct. Venous carbon dioxide pressure is 41 to 57 mm Hg against arterial 35 to 45, and venous pH is 7.31 to 7.41 against arterial 7.35 to 7.45.
Higher oxygen pressure and lower pH
The pH is right, but venous oxygen pressure is far lower, 30 to 40 mm Hg against an arterial value greater than 88.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 11, 14, 18 and 37

set2.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set2.q: A 58-year-old's arterial blood gas includes the base excess or deficit. Why is that value reported?
opts: To tell respiratory from nonrespiratory change
Correct. Base excess or deficit, the sum of the buffer anions in whole blood, is critically important in determining respiratory against nonrespiratory changes in acid-base balance.
To measure the dissolved carbon dioxide
Dissolved carbon dioxide is the partial pressure of carbon dioxide; base excess sums the buffer anions to separate respiratory from nonrespiratory change.
To measure the oxygen bound to hemoglobin
Oxygen on hemoglobin is described by the saturation; base excess is the buffer-anion sum that separates respiratory from nonrespiratory change.
To measure the carbon monoxide exposure
Carbon monoxide poisoning is indicated by carboxyhemoglobin; base excess separates respiratory from nonrespiratory change.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 40, 10 and 42

set2.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set2.q: On a 36-year-old's oxygen-hemoglobin curve shown, two stretches are bracketed. Which description fits the blood in the lower, low-pressure bracket?
opts: Pulmonary capillaries, where oxygen binds
The pulmonary capillaries sit on the high-pressure, flat upper part of the curve (the upper bracket); the low-pressure stretch is the tissue capillaries, releasing oxygen.
Pulmonary capillaries, where oxygen is released
In the pulmonary capillaries the oxygen pressure is high and oxygen binds with hemoglobin; release happens at low pressure in the tissues.
Tissue capillaries, where oxygen binds
The place is right but the action is reversed: in the tissue capillaries, at low oxygen pressure, oxygen is released from hemoglobin.
Tissue capillaries, where oxygen is released
Correct. Where the oxygen pressure is low, in the tissue capillaries, oxygen is released from hemoglobin; where it is high, in the pulmonary capillaries, oxygen binds.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 38
set2.alt: Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve with two unlabeled brackets, one high and one low on the curve

set2.io: Discuss the clinical significance of an abnormal anion gap.
set2.q: A 25-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has an anion gap of 24 (normal 9 to 15). What usually causes an elevated anion gap?
opts: A decrease in unmeasured anions
Fewer unmeasured anions would narrow the gap; an elevated gap usually means MORE of them, such as ketoacids.
An increase in unmeasured cations
More unmeasured cations, such as lithium, DECREASE the anion gap; an elevated gap usually means more unmeasured anions.
An increase in unmeasured anions
Correct. An elevated anion gap is usually due to an increase in unmeasured anions, such as ketoacids, lactate, phosphate and anionic proteins (albumin).
A loss of serum albumin
Low albumin is associated with a DECREASED gap (correct it if albumin is abnormal); an elevated gap usually reflects more unmeasured anions.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 47 and 48

set2.io: Discuss the clinical significance of an abnormal anion gap.
set2.q: A healthy 30-year-old has a normal anion gap. Which anion accounts for most of that physiologic gap?
opts: Serum albumin
Correct. The anion gap is the concentration of anions other than chloride and bicarbonate, and serum albumin accounts for most of the physiologic (normal) gap.
Lactate
Lactate contributes to the gap, with ketones, phosphate and sulfate, but albumin accounts for most of the normal gap.
Bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is measured and subtracted; the gap's anions are the others, mostly serum albumin.
Chloride
Chloride is one of the measured anions subtracted in the formula; the gap is the anions OTHER than chloride and bicarbonate, mostly albumin.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 45

set2.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set2.q: A 61-year-old has a metabolic alkalosis, and the cause is not vomiting, suction or bicarbonate given. Which electrolyte depletions are listed causes?
opts: Magnesium and albumin depletion
Magnesium and albumin belong to the anion gap's unmeasured ions; the metabolic alkalosis causes are potassium and chloride depletion.
Bicarbonate and phosphate depletion
Losing bicarbonate (base) produces metabolic ACIDOSIS; the alkalosis causes are potassium and chloride depletion.
Potassium and chloride depletion
Correct. Causes of metabolic alkalosis: base gain (excessive bicarbonate administration), acid loss (vomiting, nasogastric suction), potassium depletion and chloride depletion.
Sodium and calcium depletion
Sodium and calcium are not listed causes; the electrolyte causes of metabolic alkalosis are potassium and chloride depletion.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 34, 32 and 47

set2.io: Calculate the anion gap.
set2.q: A 67-year-old has serum sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 148 mEq/L), potassium 4.5 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L), chloride 99 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
opts: 13.5 mEq/L
13.5 also subtracts the potassium; the formula is sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate): 136 minus 118 = 18.
18 mEq/L
Correct. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 136 minus (99 plus 19) = 136 minus 118 = 18; the potassium is not in the formula.
22.5 mEq/L
22.5 adds the potassium to the sodium; the formula uses sodium alone: 136 minus 118 = 18.
37 mEq/L
37 is sodium minus chloride alone; the bicarbonate is part of the subtraction: 136 minus 118 = 18.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

set2.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set2.q: A 29-year-old is having a panic attack. Her arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 28 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg). Which process explains it?
opts: Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation retains carbon dioxide and RAISES the pressure; a low value with anxiety is hyperventilation.
Hyperventilation
Correct. Decreases in the carbon dioxide pressure are usually associated with hyperventilation, with anxiety, pain and pregnancy as clinical examples.
Obstructive lung disease
Obstructive lung disease retains carbon dioxide and raises the pressure; her low value comes from hyperventilation.
Impaired respiratory center
An impaired respiratory center (drugs, anesthesia, head trauma) raises the carbon dioxide; anxiety lowers it by hyperventilation.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 12 and 22

set2.io: Calculate the anion gap.
set2.q: A 22-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 148 mEq/L), potassium 4.0 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L), chloride 100 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is her anion gap?
opts: 22 mEq/L
22 also subtracts the potassium; the formula is sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) only: 138 minus 112 = 26.
26 mEq/L
Correct. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) = 138 minus (100 plus 12) = 26; the potassium is not part of the formula.
30 mEq/L
30 adds the potassium to the sodium; the formula uses sodium alone: 138 minus (100 plus 12) = 26.
38 mEq/L
38 is sodium minus chloride alone; the bicarbonate is part of the subtraction: 138 minus 112 = 26.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

set2.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set2.q: A 66-year-old's blood gas has been read: the pH, then each value outside its normal range. What does the step-wise approach ask next?
opts: Is the sample under 3 hours old?
Sample age is checked before analysis (a gas can only be used under 3 hours); the read ends by asking whether the labs fit the patient.
Do the labs fit the clinical presentation?
Correct. The step-wise approach: what is the pH, which lab values are outside the normal range, and do the labs fit the clinical presentation of the patient (treat the patient and not the labs)?
Does the anion gap need albumin correction?
Albumin correction belongs to reading a low anion gap; the third step of the approach is whether the labs fit the clinical presentation.
Does the saturation match the pulse oximeter?
That is not a step of the approach; after the pH and the out-of-range values comes whether the labs fit the clinical presentation.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 49 and 5

set2.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set2.q: A 52-year-old has an arterial pH of 7.22 (normal 7.35 to 7.45). How does this pH change the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
opts: Right shift: oxygen bonds more tightly
The right shift of acidosis loosens the hold: oxygen is released more easily; tighter bonding is the left shift of alkalosis.
Right shift: oxygen is released more easily
Correct. A low pH (acidosis) shifts the curve to the right, and oxygen is released more easily from hemoglobin.
Left shift: oxygen is released more easily
A left shift comes with a high pH (alkalosis) and makes oxygen bond more tightly; a low pH gives a right shift with easier release.
Left shift: oxygen bonds more tightly
This is the alkalosis pattern (high pH); a pH of 7.22 is an acidosis, which shifts the curve right and releases oxygen more easily.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 39

set2.io: Discuss indications for arterial blood gas testing.
set2.q: A 77-year-old with pneumonia is started on oxygen by nasal cannula. The team wants to know whether the oxygen therapy is working. Which arterial value answers that?
opts: Carboxyhemoglobin
Carboxyhemoglobin indicates carbon monoxide poisoning; the oxygen pressure assesses the efficacy of oxygen therapy.
Partial pressure of carbon dioxide
The carbon dioxide pressure assesses ventilation; the efficacy of oxygen therapy is assessed with the partial pressure of oxygen.
Partial pressure of oxygen
Correct. The partial pressure of oxygen is used to evaluate the ability of the lungs to oxygenate blood and to assess the efficacy of oxygen therapy.
Base excess
Base excess separates respiratory from nonrespiratory acid-base change; oxygen therapy is judged by the oxygen pressure.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 13 and 3

set2.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set2.q: A 40-year-old has been vomiting for 3 days: pH 7.50 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), carbon dioxide pressure 48 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which reading explains her carbon dioxide?
opts: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis
Correct. Metabolic alkalosis (high pH, increased bicarbonate; vomiting is a cause) is compensated by adjusting ventilation: the compensation is an increase in carbon dioxide.
Kidney compensation for a respiratory disorder
Kidney compensation adjusts bicarbonate for a respiratory problem; here the bicarbonate is the primary change and breathing compensates.
A respiratory alkalosis from vomiting
Respiratory alkalosis has a LOW carbon dioxide; hers is raised, the compensation for a metabolic alkalosis.
A primary respiratory acidosis
A primary respiratory acidosis would make the pH LOW; hers is high with a raised bicarbonate, so the carbon dioxide rise is compensation.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 52, 53, 33 and 34

mis.A respiratory alkalosis from vomiting: ruled out by the carbon dioxide

set2.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set2.q: A 45-year-old has had 5 days of profuse diarrhea: pH 7.30 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), carbon dioxide pressure 40 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which mechanism produced this picture?
opts: Loss of acid
Acid loss, as in vomiting or nasogastric suction, causes metabolic ALKALOSIS; his pH is low.
Gain of base
Base gain (excessive bicarbonate administration) causes metabolic alkalosis; his bicarbonate is decreased.
Gain of acid
Acid gain (renal failure, diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, anaerobic metabolism) is the other route to metabolic acidosis; diarrhea loses base.
Loss of base
Correct. This is metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.35, normal carbon dioxide, decreased bicarbonate), and diarrhea causes it through loss of base, as renal tubular acidosis does.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 32, 31 and 34

set2.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set2.q: A 55-year-old's arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg). Which of her conditions is a cause of a low carbon dioxide pressure?
opts: Pulmonary emboli
Correct. Causes of a low carbon dioxide pressure are hypoxia, pulmonary emboli, anxiety and pain.
A recent head injury
Head trauma impairs the respiratory center and raises the carbon dioxide pressure; pulmonary emboli are the low-value cause.
Emphysema
Emphysema is an obstructive lung disease and raises the carbon dioxide pressure; pulmonary emboli lower it.
A barbiturate overdose
Barbiturates impair the respiratory center and raise the carbon dioxide pressure; pulmonary emboli lower it.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set2.q: A 55-year-old's clinician needs the actual amount of oxygen carried in his blood, bound and dissolved together. Which blood gas value reports it?
opts: Oxygen saturation
Saturation is a ratio that indicates the relationship between oxygen and hemoglobin, not the oxygen content.
Oxygen content
Correct. Oxygen content is the actual amount of oxygen in the blood: 98% transported with hemoglobin and the remainder dissolved.
Partial pressure of oxygen
The partial pressure reflects only the oxygen dissolved in plasma, less than 2% of the oxygen carried; the content is the actual total amount.
Oxygen capacity
Oxygen capacity is the maximum amount of oxygen that can combine with hemoglobin, not the amount actually carried; that is the oxygen content.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 37, 35 and 13

set2.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set2.q: A 26-year-old who lives at sea level flies to a high mountain town and has an arterial oxygen pressure of 64 mm Hg (normal greater than 80 mm Hg). What explains it?
opts: Decreased atmospheric oxygen
Correct. Decreased atmospheric oxygen is one of the clinical examples of a decreased oxygen pressure (with insufficient inspired oxygen among its causes).
An increased fraction of inspired oxygen
An increased fraction of inspired oxygen raises the oxygen pressure; at altitude the atmospheric oxygen is decreased.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation is a cause of an INCREASED oxygen pressure; the low value at altitude is from decreased atmospheric oxygen.
Pulmonary edema
Pulmonary edema lowers the oxygen pressure too, but nothing here suggests it; the stated change is the decreased atmospheric oxygen.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 15 and 24

mis.Pulmonary edema: competing cause, not in this case

set2.io: Explain differences between arterial and venous blood gas measurements.
set2.q: A 68-year-old has just had a direct arterial stick for a blood gas. How is the puncture site managed?
opts: Ice on the site, as for the sample itself
Ice is for the SAMPLE on its way to the lab; the site needs pressure for at least 2 minutes until bleeding stops.
Pressure for at least 2 minutes, until bleeding stops
Correct. Hold pressure for a minimum of 2 minutes or longer as needed until the bleeding stops; a pressure dressing may be needed.
A plain adhesive bandage, with no pressure held
An arterial stick needs pressure held for at least 2 minutes, longer if needed, and sometimes a pressure dressing.
Pressure only for the time the needle is withdrawn
Pressure is held for a minimum of 2 minutes, longer as needed until bleeding stops, not just at withdrawal.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

set2.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set2.q: A 33-year-old's blood pH reflects the hydrogen ions from both volatile and nonvolatile acids. Which acid is the volatile one?
opts: Dietary acids
Dietary acids are nonvolatile acids, with lactic acids and ketoacids; the volatile example is carbonic acid.
Ketoacids
Ketoacids, as in diabetic ketoacidosis, are nonvolatile acids; carbonic acid is the volatile acid.
Carbonic acid
Correct. The sources of hydrogen ions are volatile acids, such as carbonic acid, and nonvolatile acids, such as dietary acids, lactic acids and ketoacids.
Lactic acid
Lactic acid is a nonvolatile acid, like dietary acids and ketoacids; the volatile acid is carbonic acid.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set2.q: A 31-year-old woman has had a respiratory alkalosis for several days. Which compensation is expected?
opts: The kidneys raise the bicarbonate
A rise in bicarbonate is the compensation for respiratory ACIDOSIS; alkalosis is compensated by a decrease.
None; only metabolic disorders compensate
Both kinds compensate: respiratory disorders through the kidney's bicarbonate (days), metabolic ones through breathing (minutes to hours).
Breathing slows to raise the carbon dioxide
The carbon dioxide is the primary problem here; compensation for a respiratory disorder comes from the kidneys adjusting bicarbonate.
The kidneys lower the bicarbonate
Correct. Respiratory disorders are compensated by the kidney adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption over days: respiratory alkalosis compensation is a decrease in bicarbonate.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 50 and 51

set2.io: Discuss indications for arterial blood gas testing.
set2.q: A 61-year-old woman is well today and is scheduled for a lung resection next week. Why might an arterial blood gas be drawn now?
opts: To establish baseline values before the operation
Correct. Establishing baseline values pre- and post-operatively is one of the indications for an arterial blood gas.
To grade the severity of her lung disease
A blood gas does NOT indicate the degree of any abnormality; severity needs a physical assessment. Here it sets a pre-operative baseline.
To monitor response to ongoing therapy
She is not on an ongoing therapy to follow; the indication here is a baseline before the operation.
To monitor her as a critically ill patient
Monitoring critically ill patients is an indication, but she is well today; the gas is drawn to establish a pre-operative baseline.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 3 and 5

mis.To monitor her as a critically ill patie: ruled out by a stated finding
mis.To monitor response to ongoing therapy: ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set2.q: A 55-year-old on a mechanical ventilator has pH 7.50 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), carbon dioxide pressure 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate 24 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is the most likely cause?
opts: Renal tubular acidosis
Renal tubular acidosis loses base and causes metabolic acidosis with a low pH; his pH is high.
Loss of gastric acid
Vomiting or nasogastric suction causes metabolic alkalosis with an increased bicarbonate; his bicarbonate is normal.
Mechanical over-ventilation
Correct. A high pH with a low carbon dioxide and normal bicarbonate is respiratory alkalosis, and mechanical over-ventilation is one of its causes.
Respiratory depression from opioids
Opioid respiratory depression raises the carbon dioxide and causes respiratory ACIDOSIS; his carbon dioxide is low.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 29, 30, 27 and 34

set2.io: Interpret arterial blood gas results.
set2.q: A 68-year-old with long-standing emphysema has pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), carbon dioxide pressure 60 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which reading fits?
opts: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Correct. Chronic respiratory acidosis results from long-standing lung disease: the carbon dioxide is high, the pH tries to normalize and the bicarbonate rises (metabolic compensation).
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis has a decreased bicarbonate; his is raised, with a high carbon dioxide driving the acidosis.
Acute respiratory acidosis without compensation
Acute respiratory acidosis has a normal bicarbonate; his is raised, the compensation that comes with long-standing disease.
Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Metabolic alkalosis has a HIGH pH; his pH is low with a high carbon dioxide, a respiratory acidosis.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 28, 27 and 51

set2.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman receiving supplemental oxygen has an arterial oxygen pressure of 145 mm Hg (normal greater than 80 mm Hg). Which factor most directly explains the high value?
opts: An intracardiac shunt
Intracardiac shunts lower the oxygen pressure; a high value on supplemental oxygen reflects the increased fraction of inspired oxygen.
Hypoventilation from neuromuscular disease
Hypoventilation secondary to neuromuscular disease is a cause of a LOW oxygen pressure; her high value comes from the inspired oxygen.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease lowers the oxygen pressure; supplemental oxygen raises it through the fraction of inspired oxygen.
An increased fraction of inspired oxygen
Correct. The oxygen pressure is directly affected by the fraction of inspired oxygen, the amount of oxygen in the air taken into the lungs, and an increased fraction raises it.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 13, 23 and 24

set2.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set2.q: A 44-year-old has pH 7.29 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), carbon dioxide pressure 41 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which disorder is this?
opts: Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis has a pH above 7.45 and a low carbon dioxide; his pH is low with a normal carbon dioxide.
Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory acidosis has a HIGH carbon dioxide; his carbon dioxide is normal and his bicarbonate low.
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis has a pH above 7.45 and an increased bicarbonate; his pH and bicarbonate are both low.
Metabolic acidosis
Correct. Metabolic acidosis: pH below 7.35, carbon dioxide normal, bicarbonate decreased.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 31, 27, 33 and 30

set2.io: Discuss the clinical significance of an abnormal anion gap.
set2.q: A 59-year-old has an elevated anion gap, and no excess of unmeasured anions is found. Which less common change can also raise the gap?
opts: A fall in serum albumin
Hypoalbuminemia is associated with a DECREASED gap; the less common cause of an elevated one is a decrease in unmeasured cations.
An increase in unmeasured cations
More unmeasured cations, as with lithium, DECREASE the anion gap; the less common cause of an elevated gap is fewer of them.
A decrease in unmeasured cations
Correct. An elevated gap is usually from more unmeasured anions and less often from a decrease in unmeasured cations, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and gamma-globulins.
Severe hyperlipidemia
Severe hyperlipidemia is associated with a DECREASED gap, by affecting the sodium and chloride estimates.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 47 and 48

set2.io: Explain differences between arterial and venous blood gas measurements.
set2.q: A 57-year-old with acute dyspnea needs to know how well his lungs are oxygenating his blood. Why is the sample taken from an artery rather than a vein?
opts: Arterial blood shows how severe the illness is
The blood gas does NOT indicate the degree of any abnormality; that needs a physical assessment of the patient. Arterial blood is chosen as the better mixture.
Venous blood has no measurable gas pressures
Venous gases are measured and have their own normal values (carbon dioxide 41 to 57 mm Hg, oxygen 30 to 40); arterial blood is the better mixture.
Venous blood is free of local effects
The reverse: venous blood is localized to the phlebotomy site and can be affected by temperature, perfusion, movement and local infection.
Arterial blood is a better mixture of blood
Correct. Arterial blood provides a better mixture of blood and indicates how well the lungs oxygenate it; venous blood is more localized to the phlebotomy site.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 5, 11 and 14

set2.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to diagnose acid-base disorders.
set2.q: A 45-year-old firefighter is brought in after smoke inhalation. Which component of the arterial blood gas order indicates the amount of carbon monoxide poisoning?
opts: Partial pressure of oxygen
The oxygen pressure measures oxygen dissolved in plasma and the lungs' ability to oxygenate; carboxyhemoglobin is what indicates carbon monoxide poisoning.
Base excess
Base excess is the sum of the buffer anions in whole blood and separates respiratory from nonrespiratory change; carboxyhemoglobin measures carbon monoxide.
Bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is the metabolic buffer, about half of the buffer anions in whole blood; the amount of carbon monoxide poisoning is read from carboxyhemoglobin.
Carboxyhemoglobin
Correct. Carboxyhemoglobin forms when hemoglobin is exposed to carbon monoxide, and its result indicates the amount of carbon monoxide poisoning.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 42, 9 and 40

set2.io: Describe expected findings in: Metabolic acidosis, Metabolic alkalosis, Respiratory acidosis, Respiratory alkalosis.
set2.q: A 60-year-old in severe acidosis has a serum potassium of 5.9 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L). What best explains the potassium?
opts: Potassium shifting from the blood into cells
The shift into the intracellular space is the alkalosis pattern and causes HYPOKALEMIA; acidosis moves potassium out of the cells.
Potassium lost through the kidneys
A loss would lower the serum potassium; in acidosis the high level comes from potassium shifting into the extracellular space.
Potassium shifting out of cells into the blood
Correct. pH changes cause changes in serum potassium: in acidosis, potassium shifts into the extracellular space, causing hyperkalemia.
Potassium depletion from the acidosis
Potassium depletion is a cause of metabolic ALKALOSIS and would lower the level; acidosis shifts potassium out of the cells.
set2.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 44 and 34
